prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Before anything could happen, flecks of real gold on her mouth, her eyes more convex than any others, the ground spoke, the barrier of lilacs spoke. What sang in the black tree was entirely gold. Her chair was empty. New absence is a great figure dark as the underskin of fruit. At the center of the earth it surrounds and amplifies the dead whose music never slows down. She came by car. I came by train. We embraced. It was at the foot of a hill steeply crowned with apples and a ruined fortress. Imagination did not make the world. Sweetness is the entire portion. Before anything could happen, happiness, the necessary precondition of the world, spoke and flowered over the hill. When I was in Hell on the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness kissed my open eyes. It felt hugely convex, seeing and immediately forgetting. By contrast, what I imagined later was nothing.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Before, What, Her

outputs.L1: Before anything could happen—flecks of real gold on her mouth, her eyes more convex than any others—the ground spoke; the barrier of lilacs spoke. What sang in the black tree was entirely gold. Her chair was empty. New absence is a great figure, dark as the underskin of fruit. At the center of the earth, it surrounds and amplifies the dead, whose music never slows. She came by car. I came by train. We embraced at the foot of a hill, steeply crowned with apples and a ruined fortress. Imagination did not make the world. Sweetness is the entire portion. Before anything could happen, happiness—the necessary precondition of the world—spoke and flowered over the hill. When I was in Hell, on the ruined palisade, either mystery or loneliness kissed my open eyes. It felt immensely convex: seeing and immediately forgetting. By contrast, what I imagined later was nothing.
outputs.L2:
Before events could begin, actual gold shimmered across her lips, and her eyes curved outward beyond all others. The earth found a voice; so did the wall of lilacs. In the darkened tree, the singing was pure gold. Her seat stood vacant. A fresh absence takes on an immense form, shadowed like the flesh beneath a fruit’s skin. Deep within the planet, it encloses the dead and magnifies them, while their music continues without ever losing speed.

She arrived in a car; I traveled there by train. We held each other. We met below a hillside that rose sharply, topped by apple trees and the remains of a fortress. The world was not created by imagination. Sweetness makes up the whole allotment.

Before anything began, happiness—the condition the world requires in order to exist—gave voice and blossomed across the hill. While I stood in Hell upon the shattered palisade, something—mystery or solitude—pressed a kiss to my uncovered eyes. The sensation was enormously rounded: to perceive and then forget at once. Compared with that, everything I pictured afterward amounted to nothing.
outputs.L3:
Before the events themselves can fully unfold, the natural world seems to speak through vivid, golden imagery, as though the landscape is preparing the way for what is to come. At the center of this scene stands an empty chair, a powerful symbol of a new and profound absence. Rather than remaining silent, that absence appears to surround and intensify the lingering “music” of the dead, making memory and loss feel even more present.

The speaker and a woman arrive separately, each by a different means, but their paths converge in an embrace. They meet beneath a hill covered with apple trees and crowned by the ruins of an old fortress, a setting that brings together fertility, history, love, and decay. Over this hill, happiness seems to flower. It is presented not merely as a passing emotion but as a necessary condition for the world itself—as though existence depends upon the possibility of joy.

Yet this happiness is interrupted by a hellish instant marked by mystery, isolation, or both. In that moment, the speaker is overwhelmed by a vision of extraordinary force. Almost immediately, however, the vision is forgotten. Its lost intensity diminishes everything that follows, so that later acts of imagination seem trivial beside the revelation that briefly appeared and then vanished.
outputs.L4:
The passage meditates on grief, absence, memory, and happiness through a sequence of surreal images drawn from the natural world. Landscapes, animals, weather, light, and darkness appear not merely as background but as expressions of an inner emotional reality. The boundaries between the external world and the speaker’s consciousness become unstable: nature seems to remember, mourn, and conceal meanings of its own. This dreamlike imagery gives shape to feelings that cannot be explained directly, especially the pain of losing someone whose presence continues to be felt.

At the center of the passage is a fragmented recollection of reunion and separation. Memory does not unfold in a clear, chronological order. Instead, it arrives in flashes—moments of recognition, intimacy, loneliness, beauty, and renewed absence. The person who has been lost seems both distant and vividly present, preserved through sensory impressions and emotional echoes. Remembering becomes a kind of encounter, but one that cannot overcome death or restore what has disappeared. The past returns only in fragments, emphasizing how grief alters time and makes absence feel permanent.

Yet the passage does not present sorrow as the whole of existence. Its encounters with natural beauty and mystery suggest that reality is richer, stranger, and more powerful than anything the imagination alone can create. Even loneliness becomes part of a larger experience of being alive. The world contains suffering and death, but it also offers moments of wonder that resist despair.

Happiness therefore emerges not as a denial of grief, nor as a simple feeling of pleasure, but as something fundamental and necessary. It is the underlying condition that makes memory, love, beauty, and even mourning possible. The passage ultimately proposes that happiness belongs to the structure of the world itself: fragile but persistent, present even in loss, and capable of surviving alongside death.
outputs.L5:
**Before Her**

Before her, the world had seemed predictable—days arriving and leaving without surprise. Then she appeared, carrying questions he had never thought to ask.

“What are you waiting for?” she said.

He searched for an answer, but found only fear disguised as patience.

She smiled and held out her hand. In that moment, he understood: what mattered was not who he had been before, but who he might become with her.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about absence, reunion, memory, and the limits of imagination, using images of gold, lilacs, fruit, apples, a ruined fortress, and Hell.
counterfactuals.output:
In the room where you were not, the chairs grew long gold roots and drank from the silence beneath the floor. Every clock forgot its hands. Lilacs opened in the cupboards, pale as bruises, filling the plates with the fragrance of a spring no one had lived.

I kept your name among the fruit.

It ripened strangely—plums darkened around it, pears became small bells, and the apples shone with the red certainty of sealed mouths. When I cut one open, I found no seeds, only a staircase descending toward the ruined fortress where memory had taken shelter.

There, the walls were weather gnawed. Gold leaf clung to the stones like the last light on a dead king’s eyelids. I walked through courtyards crowded with invisible horses. At the highest window, you stood exactly as I remembered you, which is to say: incorrectly.

We embraced, and the fortress fell upward.

For one breath, absence returned everything it had stolen—the warmth of your shoulder, the lilac dusk, the orchard trembling with its burden. Then memory altered the weather. Your face became a door I could not open. Your voice crossed the room wearing another voice.

Beyond the battlements, Hell was not fire but an endless table set for two, where the fruit never spoiled and no one arrived. The apples waited in bowls of hammered gold. Lilacs bowed from black vases. Even sorrow had been polished until it reflected nothing.

I tried to imagine us saved.

But imagination has borders, though it sends its birds across them. I could give you wings, a crown, a road out of Hell; I could rebuild the fortress stone by shining stone. I could place the lost years in your hands like peaches.

I could not make them unlost.

So we sat together in the ruin, almost reunited, while night entered the apples and the gold forgot how to gleam. Between us, absence lay down like a faithful animal.

Neither of us had the heart to send it away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental lyrical paragraph in a dreamlike, fragmented style. Include two people arriving separately by car and train, an empty chair, music beneath the earth, and happiness flowering over a hill.
counterfactuals.output: She came by car at dusk, headlights combing the wheat; he arrived later by train, carrying the station’s blue silence in his coat. Between them: an empty chair, still warm with the shape of no one. They spoke in fragments—glass, rain, remember—while beneath the earth, music turned in its sleep, a slow brass animal breathing through roots and stones. Then morning loosened its bright thread, and beyond the window happiness began flowering over the hill, yellow and impossible, opening its many mouths to the sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, enigmatic prose poem that begins by repeating “Before anything could happen” and contrasts immediate perception with imagined memory. Make the imagery strange, beautiful, and metaphysical.
counterfactuals.output:
Before anything could happen, before anything could happen, the light had already mistaken my face for a window. Through it passed a blue animal carrying the silence of bells, and I saw—at once, without history—the rain fastening its silver nerves to the earth.

But memory imagined otherwise. It placed a childhood beneath the floorboards, warm as bread and equally impossible; it invented a mother made of dusk, a garden where each pear contained a sleeping eclipse. What stood before me was only a cup, chipped at the rim, receiving noon. What I remembered was the sea rehearsing my name inside it.

Thus the instant opened its clear, merciless eye, while the past wandered behind it in robes of smoke, touching everything with hands it had never possessed. A moth struck the glass and became, for one breath, the white hinge of eternity. I watched it. I recalled it. Between those two acts, an unseen country raised its towers.

Nothing had happened. Already the ruins were luminous.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of surrealist prose centered on meeting someone at the foot of an apple-covered hill crowned by ruins. Explore death, sweetness, loneliness, and the idea that imagination did not create the world.
counterfactuals.output:
At the foot of the hill, where apples lay so thick the earth seemed to have grown a red skin, I met a woman carrying a candle in her mouth.

Above us, the ruins wore the evening like a broken crown. Every window opened onto the same empty room. Ravens flew backward through the arches.

“Are you dead?” I asked.

She bit the flame in half. “Only when I am alone.”

We began to climb. The apples whispered beneath our shoes, each one sweet with the small, private rot at its center. She handed me one, and when I bit it, I tasted summer, then childhood, then the cold iron key to a house that had never existed.

“You imagined this,” she said.

“No.”

And it was true. Imagination had not made the hill, nor the fruit, nor the ruins waiting above us with their mouths full of stars. The world had invented itself long before our loneliness arrived to misunderstand it.

At the summit, she vanished through a wall.

I remained outside, holding the bitten apple, while all around me the dead continued ripening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an uncanny literary passage with nonlinear transitions and vivid sensory images: gold on a woman’s mouth, speaking ground and lilacs, a black tree singing, an empty chair, the dead making music underground, and a kiss in Hell.
counterfactuals.output:
Gold leaf clung to the woman’s mouth. When she smiled, the room filled with the dry shimmer of coins poured onto a grave.

“Listen,” she said.

But it was the ground that answered.

Beneath the floorboards, beneath the cellar jars where peaches floated like drowned suns, the earth cleared its throat. Lilacs pushed their purple faces through the cracks and whispered in the voices of people we had forgotten. Each blossom smelled of rain, old gloves, and the moment before a name leaves the tongue forever.

Outside, a black tree was singing.

It had no leaves, no birds, no mercy. Its branches scraped the moon like a bow drawn across a single silver string. From that sound came winter; from winter came a hallway; at the end of the hallway stood an empty chair upholstered in green velvet, still warm.

No one admitted having risen from it.

Years earlier—or perhaps tomorrow—the dead began making music underground. They used rib bones for flutes, teeth for castanets, coffin nails for tuning forks. Their song trembled up through the roots of the lilacs, and the lilacs repeated it badly, sweetening each sorrow until grief became almost fragrant.

The woman touched her gilded lips to my ear.

“You promised,” she whispered.

The black tree stopped singing. The chair turned slowly toward us.

Then we were in Hell, though Hell resembled a kitchen at dawn: a cold stove, a stopped clock, one cup set out for someone who would never arrive. Ash drifted through the window like gray pollen. The woman’s gold mouth had begun to melt, bright threads running down her chin.

I kissed her.

The dead struck up a waltz beneath our feet. The ground spoke my name in a voice of lilacs. And somewhere, impossibly far above us, the empty chair creaked as if at last someone had sat down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
